document.text:
Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type with a press in Europe during the mid-fifteenth century. Scribes had previously copied books by hand, which made reproduction slow and expensive. Printing enabled many copies to be produced from one prepared set of type and decreased the cost of reproducing a book.

Cheaper, more numerous books reached a broader reading public. Printers also produced pamphlets in vernacular languages, allowing religious and political arguments to circulate more quickly than handwritten copies. The spread of printed material did not create literacy by itself, but it supported growing demand for reading and education.

Authorities responded after printed controversy had expanded. Some governments and churches required licenses or censored printers, while printers sometimes moved production to places with fewer constraints. Printing therefore changed both the speed of communication and the attempts to control it.

entities.name: Johannes Gutenberg
entities.description: Historical figure who combined movable metal type with a press in Europe during the mid-fifteenth century.

entities.name: Movable metal type
entities.description: Reusable metal type combined with a press for printing in Europe.

entities.name: Press
entities.description: A press combined with movable metal type in Gutenberg's printing process.

entities.name: Printing
entities.description: The process of producing books and other printed material from prepared type.

entities.name: Scribal copying
entities.description: The prior process of copying books by hand.

entities.name: Reproduction speed
entities.description: The speed at which books or copies are reproduced.

entities.name: Reproduction cost
entities.description: The cost of reproducing a book or making a copy.

entities.name: Prepared set of type
entities.description: A set of type from which many copies can be produced.

entities.name: Printed books
entities.description: Books produced through printing, including cheaper and more numerous copies.

entities.name: Reading public
entities.description: The broader population reached by cheaper, more numerous books.

entities.name: Pamphlets
entities.description: Short printed works produced by printers, including works in vernacular languages.

entities.name: Vernacular languages
entities.description: Local or commonly spoken languages used for pamphlets.

entities.name: Religious and political arguments
entities.description: Arguments circulated through printed pamphlets and other material.

entities.name: Literacy
entities.description: The ability or condition associated with reading, which printing supported but did not itself create.

entities.name: Demand for reading and education
entities.description: Growing demand that was supported by the spread of printed material.

entities.name: Printed controversy
entities.description: Controversy associated with printed material that expanded before authorities responded.

entities.name: Authorities
entities.description: Governments and churches that responded to expanded printed controversy.

entities.name: Licenses and censorship
entities.description: Controls imposed by some governments and churches on printers and printing.

entities.name: Printers
entities.description: Producers of printed books and pamphlets who sometimes moved production to places with fewer constraints.

entities.name: Speed of communication
entities.description: The speed at which information and arguments circulate.

entities.name: Attempts to control communication
entities.description: Efforts by authorities to regulate printed communication.
